text: {{other}} promises that a saint protects those crossing a broken footbridge. A long detour exists, which has made the promise commercially inconvenient.

outcome.text: You arrive tired by the longer road. {{other}} cannot deny that the destination improves a pilgrimage considerably.

success.text: You cross safely and gain a modest reputation for nerve. The missing boards have not been repaired by your example.

failure.text: The bridge gives way over deep water. The assurance of protection cannot keep you afloat.

effects.death: Drowned after choosing to cross a visibly broken bridge.

choices.label: Warn travellers and refuse to endorse the assurance

outcome.text: You point out the missing boards. {{other}} acquires a rival with a distressingly detailed knowledge of the miracle’s construction.

title: THE SERMON WITH YOUR MEASURES IN IT
text: {{other}} has proposed a sermon against dishonest measures using details suspiciously close to your neighbours’ accounts. You are asked to confirm the names.

outcome.text: The allegation is left out for want of evidence. {{other}} must deliver the moral point without the convenient pleasure of naming you.
You acquire a false-testimony charge. The sermon’s moral certainty has become your legal uncertainty.

choices.label: Help write a sermon without identifying households

outcome.text: The sermon keeps its argument and loses its named victim. {{other}} is disappointed by how well it still works.

title: THE BROTHER WHO WILL NOT SPEAK
text: A visiting brother remains silent while {{other}} tries to extract a public blessing. The brother quietly helps an exhausted porter lift a load instead.

choices.label: Help carry the load without arranging a ceremony

outcome.text: You take up the practical work. {{other}} joins you after discovering nobody is left to admire the refusal to speak.

choices.label: Let the useful silence remain useful

outcome.text: You gain understanding without demanding a sign. {{other}} is less annoyed once no one is watching the disappointment.

title: THE RELIC WITH TOOTH MARKS
text: {{other}} asks you to help identify a sacred bone. The household dog identifies it first and is proving difficult to cross-examine.

choices.label: Withdraw the claim until there is evidence

outcome.text: You withdraw the claim. {{other}} regards the dog as a neglected witness for the defence, though it appears principally interested in the bone.

choices.label: Turn the gathering toward ordinary alms (3g)

outcome.text: You contribute three gold to relief and gain faith. The bone’s status remains undecided while something useful happens.

title: THE WINDOW OPENED IN WINTER
text: {{other}} wants a dying neighbour visited but objects to the draught from the open door. The objection has outlasted the visitor’s strength.

outcome.text: You spend four gold on care and gain faith. {{other}} sees a useful duty completed before it can become another argument.

choices.label: Give a household blanket instead of debating the door

outcome.text: Your household loses a little wealth and gains a reputation for care. You do not claim to have cured the neighbour by being kind.

choices.label: Leave the discussion to people who have time for it

outcome.text: You avoid the expense and lose {{other}}’s respect. The unfinished duty is smaller than your explanation for leaving it.

title: THE SCAFFOLD’S BLESSING
text: {{other}} says the repaired scaffold has been blessed. The supporting peg is still lying on the ground beside the holy water.

choices.label: Fit the peg before going up

outcome.text: You fit the peg before climbing. {{other}} allows that a blessing need not be required to do the carpenter’s part as well.

choices.label: Climb before the support is fixed (risk lasting injury)

success.text: The scaffold holds and you finish the task. You collect the promised fee for a task that remains a terrible example.

failure.text: The platform gives way. The fall leaves lasting pain that does not disappear when the bruises fade.

choices.label: Refuse to test the argument with your body

outcome.text: {{other}} objects to your lack of confidence. The loose peg lies beside the platform, displaying admirable patience with both of you.

title: THE MAN WHO CAN POLISH YOUR SIGHT
text: {{other}} recommends a travelling healer who promises to polish your sight with an abrasive paste. The demonstration is being performed on a spoon.

choices.label: Refuse the treatment and rest your eyes

outcome.text: You gain a little health by resting. Any existing eye condition remains; the spoon’s recovery proves nothing about yours.

choices.label: Submit to the abrasive treatment (permanent eye damage)

outcome.text: The paste injures your eyes. Failing sight becomes a lasting disability, and {{other}} loses your trust.

choices.label: Demand evidence from a patient rather than cutlery

outcome.text: You ask when the polished spoon last needed to recognise its family. {{other}} finds the demonstration less persuasive under questioning.

title: THE WORK THAT WILL NOT SWEAT ITSELF
text: While you are feverish, {{other}} insists a hard day’s labour will drive the sickness out. You would prefer it to leave by a door that does not require lifting.

choices.label: Rest and accept a lost day’s work

outcome.text: You recover some health and lose a little work performance. The existing illness remains subject to its real course.

choices.label: Work through the fever (risk making it worse)

outcome.text: The effort worsens the fever. {{other}} praises your determination until asked whether determination will also lift you out of bed.

choices.label: Pay for practical help and keep resting (7g)

outcome.text: You pay for help and recover some strength without pretending the payment itself removes the disease.

title: THE SHORTCUT WITHOUT THE ROAD
text: {{other}} offers to show you a quicker descent through an abandoned quarry. It is certainly shorter; the question is whether you arrive in one piece.

outcome.text: You take the ordinary road. {{other}} calls it timid while walking over a surface that has the courtesy to remain underfoot.

choices.label: Take the narrow ledge (risk a fatal fall)

success.text: You reach the bottom unharmed and gain confidence. {{other}} claims the loose stones were part of the intended route.

failure.text: The ledge crumbles beneath you. The shorter route has no place to stop the fall.

effects.death: Killed after choosing a dangerous shortcut through an abandoned quarry.

choices.label: Turn back before the descent begins

outcome.text: You give up the excursion and preserve your health. {{other}} keeps the story of the shortcut for a more agreeable audience.

title: THE WHITE DUST UNDER THE LID
text: {{other}} asks you to open a hot lime vessel without waiting for it to cool. The warning on the lid is inconveniently short and clear.

choices.label: Wait for proper cooling and protection

outcome.text: You wait for the safe handling. {{other}} concedes that impatience is cheaper than a burn only until somebody obeys it.
You suffer real burns and lose health. {{other}} can no longer call the warning an excess of caution.

title: THE FERRY’S EXTRA PASSENGER
text: {{other}} asks you to board a ferry already low in the water. The ferryman argues that the extra fare will make the crossing worthwhile.

outcome.text: You miss the busy part of the market and lose a little work performance. Your feet remain on the useful side of the river.

success.text: The ferry reaches the bank. You gain a small reputation for nerve and remain unable to spend it on better buoyancy.

failure.text: The overloaded boat capsizes in deep water. The extra fare cannot purchase a shore.

effects.death: Drowned after choosing an overloaded ferry.

choices.label: Pay to leave a cargo bundle behind (7g)

outcome.text: You pay to leave a bundle behind. The ferryman reluctantly accepts that cargo can survive the inconvenience of missing a crossing.

title: THE TWO IDENTICAL HERB BUNDLES
text: {{other}} has mixed up two bundles of herbs, one soothing and one violently unsuitable for supper. The labels were left in the other basket.

choices.label: Discard both and buy known food (4g)

outcome.text: You buy ordinary food and discard the doubtful herbs. {{other}} laments a supper that will produce no medical discovery.
The experiment causes gut sickness and costs you health. {{other}} learns the result without sharing the method.
You refuse the gamble and gain some judgement. Not every uncertain meal needs a conclusive ending.

title: THE BENCH BESIDE THE HEARTH
text: {{other}} has moved a small workbench beside the hearth while your bone heals. It is useful, and almost tactful enough not to mention being useful.

choices.label: Accept the help and work gently

outcome.text: You gain a little health and deepen trust with {{other}}. The broken bone remains real; the day becomes less difficult.

choices.label: Refuse to be treated as injured

outcome.text: You push too hard and lose health. {{other}} leaves the bench nearby without requiring you to admit anything.

title: THE CURE THAT IS MOSTLY A CHAIR
text: {{other}} recommends a chair beside the fire for your lasting pain. It is the first proposed remedy not accompanied by a promise to make you entirely new.

choices.label: Take the chair and accept limited relief

outcome.text: Your health improves a little while the chronic pain remains. {{other}} is good enough company not to call this a miracle.

choices.label: Keep working and refuse the fuss

outcome.text: You lose some health and gain a little work experience. The disability is neither cured nor turned into a moral failing.

title: THE TONIC WITH A FUNERAL GUARANTEE
text: {{other}} recommends a tonic whose seller promises a refund if it fails. The refund must be claimed in person, after burial.

outcome.text: You ask to see the guarantee in writing. {{other}} discovers a pressing appointment with someone who has not asked that question.
The tonic is useless and makes you feel worse. {{other}} points to the guarantee’s requirement that a deceased customer claim in person.

choices.label: Read the condition to the waiting customers

outcome.text: You expose the trick and gain public standing. {{other}} is embarrassed to have supplied such a precise recommendation.

title: THE SICKROOM’S EXCELLENT WITNESS
text: {{other}} offers to swear you have recovered enough to work, even though your health is still poor. The employer is prepared to believe whoever costs less.

choices.label: Give an honest account of your limits

outcome.text: You lose work performance and gain trust with {{other}} by refusing a useful falsehood. Your health remains a fact rather than a certificate.
The declaration reaches the employer before your strength does. The fraud complaint is much more capable of standing up than you are.

charge.offence: Submitting a knowingly false fitness declaration

title: THE BANDAGE TIED TO A PROMISE
text: {{other}} helps dress your wound and asks you to remember the favour when less frightened. The knot is firmer than the request.

choices.label: Promise practical help when you are able

outcome.text: You gain a little health and a trustworthy bond. The wound remains under care rather than vanishing under a promise.

choices.label: Pay fairly instead of owing a favour (5g)

outcome.text: You pay five gold for the help and recover some strength. {{other}} accepts a small, completed kindness.

choices.label: Accept the help and dismiss the obligation

outcome.text: You gain some health and lose trust. {{other}} tightens the final knot in silence.

title: THE MAN WHO WILL CATCH THUNDER
text: {{other}} has arranged a public demonstration with an iron pole on a high roof during a storm. The fee for holding the pole is described as hazard money only after you ask.

choices.label: Refuse the roof and warn the onlookers

outcome.text: You step away and describe the danger. {{other}} calls the crowd’s increasing distance a disappointing failure of confidence.

choices.label: Hold the pole through the storm (risk death)

success.text: The worst of the storm passes elsewhere. You earn twenty gold for a demonstration that has proved nothing safe.

failure.text: Lightning strikes the exposed roof. The promised hazard payment is no defence against it.

effects.death: Killed while knowingly holding an iron pole on a roof during a storm.

title: THE INHERITANCE THAT REQUIRES AN ADVANCE
text: {{other}} brings news of a vast foreign inheritance. The messenger requires an advance, a travel bond and your patience about the absence of a named deceased.

choices.label: Ask for an identified estate and witnesses

outcome.text: You ask for the estate’s name before paying. {{other}} becomes less certain which country contains the fortune.

choices.label: Borrow heavily to fund the supposed claim

outcome.text: You record a sixty-gold debt and lose household wealth meeting the costs. No inheritance arrives to recognise the trouble you have taken.

choices.label: Give the demand to the clerk

outcome.text: You expose the scheme and gain public standing. {{other}} becomes a rival who can now name at least one person involved.

title: THE STATUE WITH A SORE THROAT
text: {{other}} shows you a statue said to speak through a hole in the wall. Behind the wall, somebody asks for water in exactly the statue’s voice.

choices.label: Open the door before the next revelation

outcome.text: You expose the trick and gain reputation. {{other}} is annoyed that the revelation has acquired a visible speaker.

choices.label: Leave without making the frightened audience a joke

outcome.text: You preserve your own judgement and gain faith through restraint. {{other}} is grateful for less discretion than they wanted.

choices.label: Offer a more convincing voice for a dishonest fee

outcome.text: You earn seven gold and a fraud charge. Your best performance now comes with a witness behind the wall.

charge.offence: Taking payment for a staged sacred revelation

title: THE HOUSE BUILT ROUND A BONE
text: {{other}} owns a sea creature’s enormous bone and wants to charge people to touch it for luck. The carpenter thinks it would make an excellent lintel.

choices.label: Study the bone without buying the promised luck

outcome.text: You learn something about its scale and improve your bond with {{other}}. The bone remains remarkable without an extra power.
Your contribution improves the family’s public standing. The contribution supports a display, not a miracle.

title: THE GAME WITH A KING WHO CANNOT LEAVE
text: {{other}} teaches you a foreign board game in which the king moves very little and everyone else is sacrificed around him. The explanation attracts an uncomfortable number of courtiers.

choices.label: Learn the game without supplying an allegory

outcome.text: {{other}} shows you why the wooden king cannot simply order the board rearranged. You learn more than either of you intended about government.

choices.label: Explain which actual people the pieces resemble

outcome.text: Your comparison amuses the audience. {{other}} had not expected a wooden monarch to require a public defence.

title: THE DEVIL HAS TAKEN THE AFTERNOON OFF
text: The person playing the devil in a pageant has refused to perform until paid. {{other}} asks you to explain to the crowd why virtue has nothing left to conquer.

choices.label: Pay the performer what the organiser owes (9g)

outcome.text: The devil is paid and returns to work. {{other}} finds nine gold a surprisingly efficient instrument of salvation.

choices.label: Rewrite the ending around a missing adversary

outcome.text: You give the remaining virtues a quarrel among themselves. {{other}} discovers that goodness can fill an afternoon without paying a devil.

choices.label: Blame the absent performer before the crowd

outcome.text: You damage {{other}}’s trust and lose public standing for turning an unpaid wage into a moral failing.

title: THE CASTLE THAT FITS IN A CHEST
text: {{other}} shows you a beautifully made model castle with working gates. It defends a table far more effectively than several actual castles defend their villages.

choices.label: Ask how the little gates were made

outcome.text: You gain practical experience and a warm bond with {{other}}. An evening passes without anybody trying to conquer anything.

choices.label: Ask how much grain the model has protected

outcome.text: {{other}} shuts the tiny gate. It is the first part of the castle that has actually managed to keep you out.

title: THE WORD FOR COMING HOME
text: {{other}} returns from a long journey and tries to explain a word for the relief of reaching a place that knows you. The closest translation takes the rest of supper.

choices.label: Let the explanation take as long as it needs

outcome.text: {{other}} explains the word slowly, then stops translating and asks for more bread. You understand that part without help.

choices.label: Share household food and let the word remain foreign

outcome.text: You give up a little food and gain a warm acquaintance. Some meanings travel more easily in company than in words.

title: THE BAILIFF’S FOURTH CHICKEN
text: The bailiff demands a hen that your household has never owned. Your family contact has the old rent tally.

outcome.text: You and your neighbour prove the tally. The hen remains imaginary; the debt does not grow.
The bailiff pays you three coins to hide his extra assessment. Your household loses more grain than those coins could buy.

title: THE GUILD’S SMALL PRINT
text: Your family’s commission includes a penalty for hammer noise after compline. The church commissioned the bell.

choices.label: Ask {{contact}} to check the guild exemption

outcome.text: Your guild contact finds the exemption. The household keeps its fee.

choices.label: Keep the noise penalty secret for three gold

outcome.text: You pocket three gold while the workshop pays the penalty. {{contact}} learns whose silence was purchased.

title: THE RIVAL’S SHORT BUSHEL
text: The household’s rival sells grain in a bushel with a false bottom. Your parent asks you to watch the measure.

choices.label: Ask {{contact}} to witness the false measure

outcome.text: You bring witnesses and protect the household’s buyers. The rival now knows your name.

choices.label: Take three gold from the short-measure seller

outcome.text: The seller buys your silence. Your household’s buyers discover the short grain and blame the family name.

title: THE LAY SCRIBE’S BABY
text: A visiting friar mistakes your lay scribe parent for a vowed cleric and prepares a scandal of magnificent proportions.

outcome.text: The marriage entry settles it. The friar must find his scandal elsewhere.

choices.label: Sell the friar a rumour for three gold

outcome.text: The friar pays for a scandal about your own lay household. The correction will cost considerably more than three gold.

title: THE RATION HEIR
text: The garrison refuses to feed a soldier’s child until the child can carry a spear. The spear is taller than the clerk.

choices.label: Ask {{contact}} to cite the service oath

outcome.text: Your household contact quotes the service oath. You receive bread and an enemy in the stores.

choices.label: Take three gold to abandon the ration claim

outcome.text: The stores clerk buys your silence. Your family gives up a season of bread for your private handful of coins.

title: THE COUSIN’S LITTLE MAP
text: A cousin has drawn the family boundary through your nursery. The steward offers to charge you rent.

choices.label: Ask {{contact}} to compare the boundary charter

outcome.text: You compare the charter with the stones. The cousin loses a field and a little affection.

choices.label: Accept three gold to hide the cousin’s map

outcome.text: Your cousin buys your silence and presses the boundary claim. The household discovers your price was lower than the surveyor’s.

title: THE NURSERY PRECEDENT
text: Your older sibling claims the whole nursery under a succession custom invented before breakfast.

choices.label: Ask the guardian to settle nursery precedence

outcome.text: Your guardian divides the room. The throne remains undivided and very far away.

choices.label: Sell your sibling the secret nursery key

outcome.text: Your sibling pays three gold for the nursery key. The guards change the locks and your household’s opinion of you.

title: THE FLOODED STRIP
text: {{guardian}} finds seed floating across a neighbour’s boundary. {{contact}} remembers where the old ditch ran.

outcome.text: The reopened ditch saves seed on both strips. {{contact}} records your household’s share of the labour.

choices.label: Charge the neighbour for your own lost seed

outcome.text: Your false claim wins a few coins and leaves {{guardian}} to repair the damaged neighbourly agreement.

title: THE WINTER WOOD
text: {{contact}} offers fallen wood if your household helps mend the common gate before winter.

outcome.text: The common gate stands through winter. {{contact}} delivers the promised fallen wood.
The missing timber leaves the common gate open. {{contact}} charges your household for its replacement.

title: THE CUSTOMER’S SEAL
text: {{guardian}} has a commission without a deposit. {{contact}} recognises the customer’s disputed seal.

outcome.text: The witnessed deposit pays for material before the customer can dispute the order.

choices.label: Copy the seal onto another order

outcome.text: The copied seal is discovered on the second order. {{contact}} keeps it as evidence against your household.

title: THE GUILD FEAST
text: {{contact}} invites your household to show a trial piece. The entry fee will buy a week’s supper.

outcome.text: The modest sample gives the workshop a place at the feast without emptying its supper pot.
The borrowed trial piece is recognised. Your workshop pays the entry fee and loses the guild’s trust.

title: THE SHIPMENT AT THE FORD
text: {{guardian}} must choose between a safe crossing fee and a cheap flooded ford. {{contact}} has a wagon there too.

outcome.text: Both wagons share the safe crossing and split the fee. The shipment arrives with its partners intact.
{{contact}} finds the dangerous ford and learns who gave the directions. Your household loses a trading partner.

title: THE LEDGER’S SECOND HAND
text: A rival disputes {{guardian}}’s ledger. {{contact}} offers to witness a recount in the market.

choices.label: Carry both copies to the recount

outcome.text: The recount establishes what was delivered. The rival must challenge a witnessed account.

choices.label: Remove the page that favours the rival

outcome.text: The missing ledger page becomes the rival’s strongest evidence. Your household bears the cost of your bargain.

title: THE BORROWED MANUSCRIPT
text: {{guardian}} owes the priory a manuscript. {{contact}} finds rain beneath the reading-room window.

choices.label: Help dry and recopy the damaged leaves

outcome.text: The dried leaves and careful copies satisfy the priory. Your lay household retains its access to the books.
The visiting household produces witnesses. Your own household pays for the damaged manuscript.

title: THE CHARITY BREAD
text: {{contact}} asks your household to record bread for hungry neighbours. One loaf remains after the tally.

outcome.text: The checked names reveal a hungry neighbour missed from the tally. The last loaf reaches them.

choices.label: Sell the extra loaf and alter the list

outcome.text: The altered bread list is traced to your hand. Your household must replace what the charity lost.

title: THE OLD CAMPAIGN CLOAK
text: {{guardian}} offers a service cloak for your first training. {{contact}} notices an unpaid campaign receipt in its lining.

choices.label: Return the receipt to the pay clerk

outcome.text: The pay clerk acknowledges the old receipt and credits the service household.
The extra ration is refused when {{contact}} checks the muster. Your household’s genuine claim is delayed.

title: THE GARRISON’S HORSE
text: {{contact}} needs someone to hold a nervous horse while {{guardian}} checks its harness.

choices.label: Help check the girth and stay beside it

outcome.text: The checked girth holds and the garrison records your household’s help.

choices.label: Tell the quartermaster another child lost it

outcome.text: The quartermaster finds your false account beside the harness. Your household loses standing with the stores.

title: THE EMPTY TUTOR’S PURSE
text: {{guardian}} must meet a tutor’s fee and a tenant’s request for seed. {{contact}} has the household accounts.

choices.label: Read the accounts before asking for more

outcome.text: The accounts show what can be spent on tutors after seed is reserved. Your guardian trusts you with the next petition.
The hidden petition is found. The tenants blame your household for a refusal it never openly made.

title: THE COUSIN AT TABLE
text: {{contact}} brings a cousin’s challenge to your household’s precedence. {{guardian}} asks you to carry the family record.

outcome.text: The family record settles precedence without an insult. Your cousin has less reason to press another grievance.

choices.label: Alter the cousin’s place in the record

outcome.text: The altered genealogy reaches {{contact}}. The cousin keeps a copy and begins a more serious challenge.

title: THE TWO NURSERY SEALS
text: {{guardian}} finds rival nursery orders signed by different palace factions. {{contact}} asks which order you carried.

choices.label: Show both seals to the guardian

outcome.text: Both nursery seals reach the guardian. Conflicting orders are corrected before the guards choose sides.

choices.label: Tell each faction the other threatened you

outcome.text: The two palace factions compare your stories. Both now have grounds to distrust your household’s word.

title: THE HEIR’S LESSON
text: {{guardian}} arranges a lesson beside your elder sibling. {{contact}} says guards have begun wagering on which of you will rule.

choices.label: Share the lesson and refuse the wager

outcome.text: The shared lesson gives the guards no wager to collect. Your guardian records a rare quiet agreement between heirs.

choices.label: Buy a guard’s rumour about your sibling

outcome.text: The purchased rumour reaches your sibling. A nursery quarrel acquires a guard willing to repeat it.

title: THE FIRST HOUSEHOLD WORDS
text: s=>{const id=s.world.characters[s.playerCharacterId].guardianIds?.find(id2=>s.world.characters[id2]?.alive);const guardian=id?s.world.characters[id]:void 0;return`${guardian?.name??"Someone caring for you"} counts cups at supper. You repeat the word for cup with greater confidence than accuracy.`}

outcome.text: Your household gains a small voice in its nightly accounting. The cups remain easier to count than the debts.

choices.label: Insist the cat is also a cup

outcome.text: The cat refuses to join the crockery. Your household repeats the word more slowly.

title: RAIN OVER THE CRADLE
text: Rain finds a gap over your bedding. The household has one dry blanket and several strong opinions about the roof.

choices.label: Carry a small bowl to catch the rain

outcome.text: The bowl catches a little water. Your guardian praises the help and moves your bedding somewhere dry.

choices.label: Ask to share the dry blanket

outcome.text: Your guardian folds the dry blanket around you. The roof will require a less comfortable remedy.

title: YOUR RIVAL HAS HIRED A DRUMMER
text: {{rival.name}} marches into the market behind a drummer and announces that you fight like a wet pillow. A merchant offers a 30g prize if you win. Your rival demands a 10g entry wager. The drummer has learned exactly one beat.

choices.label: Take the challenge (10g)
choices.hint: Play a four-exchange duel. Win: 30g prize and duel honours. Lose or yield: your wager is gone. Injuries and reputation are at stake.

stakes.summary: Wager paid: 10g. Win the 30g purse and duel honours. Lose or yield: no refund; injury and reputation loss.

outcome.text: The merchant holds your wager. The drummer discovers a second beat. You step into the ring.

choices.label: Challenge the drummer to learn a second beat

outcome.text: The crowd laughs. The drummer stops. Your rival must now provide their own dramatic entrance.

choices.label: Keep your gold and walk away

outcome.text: You leave the wet-pillow debate to the experts. Your purse remains undefeated.

title: THE GRAIN CART CHAMPION
text: {{challenger.name}} blocks the grain cart and demands a fight before letting it pass. The driver offers you 12g to clear the road. The challenger has painted a crown on a bucket and is wearing it.

choices.label: Fight for the grain
choices.hint: Win: 12g and +15 Stores. Lose or yield: −10 Stores. Normal duel honours, injury and reputation also apply.

stakes.summary: Win: 12g and +15 Stores. Lose or yield: −10 Stores. Duel honours, injury and reputation also apply.

outcome.text: The driver lends you a blunted sword. The bucket king lowers the royal visor.
You lead the cart around the field. One sack gets soaked. The bucket king is left ruling an empty road.

title: THE WANDERING MONK
text: The travelling monk asks the children to copy “Do not waste parchment.” He has written it on a fresh sheet so large that even the back row can see the irony.

choices.label: Learn the letters, including the expensive ones

outcome.text: You learn enough letters to read the warning yourself. The monk lets you keep a scrap and looks away while you practise.

choices.label: Spend the lesson with Sir Quackbeard

outcome.text: The goose offers no instruction and requires no parchment. You enjoy the company, though the writing remains unread.

choices.label: Introduce the frog to the lesson

outcome.text: The frog leaves a wet impression on the page. You gain a reputation for mischief and the monk gains a very brief pupil with excellent jumping prospects.

title: A MOUNTAIN OF TURNIPS
text: {{father}} points out the rows waiting to be weeded. “You can see the end,” {{father}} says, omitting that the end is also where tomorrow begins.

choices.label: Work through the rows with your father

outcome.text: You finish tired and gain your father’s affection. The last row earns a quiet nod that nobody else would recognise as a celebration.

choices.label: Do enough, then hide in the hay

outcome.text: The nap is excellent. Your father’s disappointment is less restful and follows you indoors.

title: THE MILLER’S BIG SON
text: {{other}} collects lunches on behalf of the miller’s big son. The supposed protection consists of not being bothered by the people collecting it.

success.text: You refuse to surrender lunch. {{other}} backs down and remembers exactly who made the collection difficult.

failure.text: You are knocked into the ditch. {{other}} keeps the food and acquires a rival who will remember more than the price of lunch.

choices.label: Surrender the lunch and keep the afternoon quiet

outcome.text: You hand over the food. {{other}} gains confidence in the arrangement and loses some of your trust.
The goose drives {{other}} back by refusing to negotiate about ankles. The collection stops here, and the collector becomes a named rival.

title: THE QUACK DOCTOR
text: {{other}} offers a heated “healing stone” for six gold. The stone is ordinary; the explanation of its value requires a much rarer temperature.

outcome.text: You pay for a warm stone and a rest beside the brazier. The rest helps a little; no illness is cured by the salesmanship.

choices.label: Ask what happens when the stone cools

outcome.text: {{other}} recommends another appointment. You decline with a better understanding of which part of the treatment needs constant warming.
You take the stone and create a theft complaint. It remains ordinary, but your legal record is now more interesting.

charge.offence: Taking a healer’s goods without payment

title: A RAT IN THE GRANARY
text: {{other}} has declared the granary’s rat an unofficial watchman because it frightens mice. The arrangement is paid entirely in your household’s winter grain.

choices.label: Remove the rat and mend the opening

outcome.text: You drive the rat out and repair the gap, losing a little blood to the work. Household stores and security improve under a watchman that is now a plank.
The household loses stored food and {{other}} likes you better. The rat’s performance improves in exactly the wrong direction.

choices.label: Blame Sir Quackbeard for the arrangement

outcome.text: You blame the goose and lose its affection. The opening remains unmended, so the household’s stores continue to suffer.

title: THE LORD’S TOURNEY
text: The tourney steward offers a discount entry because the horse is small. The opposing knight has not been discounted, which seems a serious omission.

choices.label: Enter the uneven joust (5g; risk injury)

success.text: You unhorse the opponent and earn a net eight gold after the entry fee. The steward objects only to how many people saw the small horse win.

failure.text: You land badly and leave with a real broken bone. The steward assures you that the entry fee included the fall.

choices.label: Sell pies where the losers come down

outcome.text: You earn nine gold supplying an audience with no shortage of dramatic landings. The best customers eat without taking their eyes off the field.

choices.label: Watch the horsemanship from the safe end

outcome.text: You study the riders without entering. A little judgement is gained without giving the healer a new customer.

title: CONFESSION TIME
text: The priest asks whether you have wronged anyone. You begin with a harmless example; the priest asks why you rehearsed that one first.

choices.label: Confess the inconvenient part as well

outcome.text: You admit the truth and gain faith. The admission does not settle debts or erase charges; it merely stops the priest waiting for the missing part.
You offer the account of a person nobody in the room has met. The priest hears you out, and you keep a secret about the omission.

choices.label: Give alms without pretending they answer the question (4g)

outcome.text: You give four gold and gain some faith. The priest accepts the donation and repeats the question, now that you have finished changing the subject.

title: A WANDERING KNIGHT
text: A travelling knight seeks someone to carry armour, remember messages and receive blame in that order. He calls the post an education, which suggests the wages will be small.

success.text: He grunted approval. You are on the path to knighthood, or at the very least to heavy lifting.

failure.text: He looked you up and down, sighed, and chose the blacksmith’s daughter instead.

choices.label: Ask what the work actually pays

outcome.text: You insist on a clear wage and receive five gold for a day carrying equipment. The knight leaves without an oath from you.

choices.label: Decline the offer without a quarrel

outcome.text: You decline the post. The road remains open, and you have not promised to carry someone else’s mistakes.

title: AN UNCANNY STREAK
text: You keep winning at dice. The other players have reached the point of blaming sorcery rather than their own arithmetic, a stage at which leaving may be the cleverest throw.

choices.label: Ride the luck for all it is worth

success.text: You cleaned out the whole table and walked home whistling, pockets jingling.

failure.text: Your luck finally blinked. You lost the lot, and a tooth, to a sore loser.

outcome.text: You pocketed your winnings and left. The gamblers glared; fortune, like milk, can turn.

title: A CRUEL WINTER
text: The cold settles deep in your frail chest, as it always does. The herb-wife eyes you with pity and a price.

outcome.text: The tonic was vile and dear, but you saw the spring. For a sickly soul, that is a victory. The herb-wife now greets you by name across the market, which is not the compliment it sounds like.

success.text: You wrapped in every blanket you own and outlasted the cold. Barely.

failure.text: The fever took hold and very nearly took you. You emerge in spring, hollow-eyed, with a cough that never entirely leaves.

title: THE SWEATING SICKNESS
text: A real fever has reached your household. The herb-wife is frank about what she can attempt, which makes her prices less comforting and her advice more credible.

outcome.text: Her tonic is bitter but swift. The fever breaks before it can take root.

success.text: You sweated through three foul nights and woke clear-eyed. Spared, this time.

failure.text: The fever digs in for the long haul. This sickness will not pass quickly.

title: THE REEVE COMES KNOCKING
text: The reeve’s men bring questions about your misdeeds. One has brought irons in case the answers prove inconvenient; the other has brought a receipt book.

outcome.text: A heavy purse changes hands. The reeve discovers he was quite mistaken. Funny, that.

success.text: Out the back and over three fences. Free, filthy, and faster than you look.

failure.text: They caught you at the treeline and clapped you in irons.

outcome.text: You go quietly. The dungeon door clangs shut behind you.

title: A MATCH IS PROPOSED
text: A matchmaker offers an introduction to someone kind, capable and tired of being valued by the contents of a dowry chest. Consent, rather than a wedding, is the first business.

choices.label: Consent to the proposed household match

outcome.text: You marry by mutual consent and welcome a real spouse into the household. The settlement begins a life together, not a transfer of somebody’s belongings.
You spurned the match, eyes fixed on a grander union. Ambitious. Possibly foolish.

choices.label: Decline the match without insulting the suitor

outcome.text: You refuse kindly and leave the other person free to choose another life. No animal is required to explain the decision.

title: AN INVITATION TO THE HALL
text: You are invited to the high table after an account of your wit reaches the steward. It arrives slightly improved. You must now live up to something you never quite said.

success.text: You had them roaring with laughter. The lord himself toasted you. Doors are opening.

failure.text: You used the wrong spoon, then the wrong fork, then insulted a baroness. A long carriage ride home.

outcome.text: You said little and watched much. You now know who hates whom, and that is power.

title: A RIVAL AT COURT
text: {{other}} dismisses your success as an accident of useful acquaintances. The charge is delivered to as many useful acquaintances as possible.

choices.label: Expose the contradiction in the rumour

success.text: You make {{other}} answer for the contradictory story. Your reputation rises and the rivalry becomes explicit.

failure.text: Your trap contradicts your own account. {{other}} gains an advantage and a clearer reason to keep the rivalry alive.

choices.label: Buy a pause in the rumour (12g)

outcome.text: You pay twelve gold and gain a brief respite. {{other}} learns that silence has a price worth remembering.
You demand an answer before witnesses. {{other}} becomes a named rival instead of a rumour without an address.

title: A NOBLE PROPOSAL
text: {{other}} proposes a marriage of mutual advantage and asks what sort of life you would want beyond the advantage. It is the first question not answered by the settlement.

outcome.text: You marry into a better-connected household. Your standing can improve through that connection; no title is granted merely by the wedding.
You refuse the match graciously. Your reputation improves because you leave the proposal as private as it can still be.

title: THE NIGHT VIGIL
text: To be dubbed a knight you must keep an overnight vigil in the cold chapel, armour on, praying till dawn.

success.text: You knelt unmoving till dawn, half-frozen and wholly resolved. The bishop is impressed.

failure.text: You nodded off and clattered to the floor at midnight. Mortifying, but you finished anyway.

choices.label: Sneak a flask of wine for warmth

outcome.text: The wine kept you warm and the vigil bearable. The bishop suspects nothing. The goose would be proud.

title: A CHALLENGE OF HONOUR
text: Sir Roderick produces a glove for a challenge of honour. The careful preparation suggests he has been finding the original quarrel insufficiently productive.

choices.label: Accept the duel (risk a serious cut)

success.text: You disarm Roderick and stop with the weapon at his throat. He remains alive, humiliated and much less likely to call the next quarrel accidental.

failure.text: Roderick cuts you badly. The injury is real; your refusal to pretend it was a victory earns a small measure of respect.

outcome.text: You called the challenge childish and walked away. Some respect the restraint. Roderick crows victory.

choices.label: Propose a contest of wits instead

outcome.text: You out-argued him so thoroughly the crowd laughed Roderick out of the square. A bloodless rout.

title: THE LORD’S SUMMONS
text: Your liege calls a muster over a disputed river crossing. The written claim is dry; the crossing, you are warned, will not be.

choices.label: Ride to war for your liege

outcome.text: You don your armour and ride out. The road to glory is muddy and smells of fear.
You paid scutage to avoid the muster. Pragmatic, if not glorious. Some call it cowardice.

title: THE PEASANTS’ PETITION
text: Tenants bring a petition against a levy assessed on roofs, including two roofs that fell in last winter. Your steward calls the assessment consistent.

choices.label: Fund relief from the harsh assessment

outcome.text: You pay for relief and improve loyalty. Your household gives up coin and stores; the tenants receive an answer they can survive.
Your coffers grow as household loyalty and stores fall. The cruelty is recorded in your reputation rather than blamed on a parent who may not be alive.

choices.label: Offer a smaller assessment and clear terms

outcome.text: You take a smaller return and improve loyalty. People can plan around an amount that no longer changes with the steward’s mood.

title: A WHISPER OF TREASON
text: Plotters invite you to lend your name and evidence against a powerful baron. They promise to share the reward and are less exact about whose neck secures the attempt.

success.text: Your evidence reaches the council and the plotters pay you fifty gold. The baron faces an inquiry; no new title has yet been granted.

failure.text: The plot was betrayed. Guards drag you to the block at dawn.

effects.death: Beheaded for treason. The crowd, as ever, brought pies.

choices.label: Betray the plotters to the baron

outcome.text: You sold them out. The baron rewards your "loyalty" handsomely, though you sleep with one eye open now.

choices.label: Refuse without inventing a later victory

outcome.text: You keep your name off the conspiracy. What the plotters do next is theirs; your legal record does not acquire their plan.

title: BUILDING A LEGACY
text: A mason offers a public dedication worthy of your wealth. The relief wardens ask whether the money might also do something for people who cannot read the inscription.

choices.label: Fund chapel relief and a public dedication (40g)

outcome.text: You endow relief associated with the chapel. Food security and Church standing improve; the dedication does not pretend a new building rose in an afternoon.

choices.label: Fund care for the sick and poor (40g)

outcome.text: You pay for practical relief and improve public health conditions. The people doing the work receive supplies rather than an expensive drawing of a hospital.

choices.label: Keep the reserve for your household

outcome.text: You retain the money and improve the household’s food reserve by careful planning. There will be no inscription recording the choice.

title: A PEDLAR OF RELICS
text: A pedlar offers a supposedly angelic feather. The story is magnificent; the object is the sort a barnyard bird leaves without an audience.

outcome.text: You bought the feather and prayed over it nightly. Faith asks no questions. Strangely, you feel comforted.

success.text: You show why the feather is an ordinary bird’s feather. Your reputation improves and {{other}} loses your trust rather than vanishing from the town.

failure.text: Your objection fails to convince the onlookers. {{other}} keeps the advantage and you keep the memory of being contradicted by people who never examined the feather.

outcome.text: You take the feather for Sir Quackbeard, who does not recognise a need to have it back. {{other}} has a genuine theft to complain about.

charge.offence: Taking a relic seller’s goods without payment

title: A CALLING TO THE CLOISTER
text: The abbot offers you holy orders, long work and a small place in a community that will know when you are avoiding either. You are allowed time to answer.

outcome.text: You take holy orders and gain Church standing. The vows do not appoint you to a paid post; service and qualifications must still earn one.
You decline the vows and offer practical service. The abbot accepts an honest answer more readily than a beautiful promise.

title: A VILLAGER CRIES MIRACLE
text: A child’s recovery is being attributed to your nearby prayer. The people praising you have forgotten the person who carried water through the night.

choices.label: Accept the attention and its donations

outcome.text: You receive donations and public standing. The prayer is remembered, together with your willingness to stand beside its collection bowl.

choices.label: Credit the care and decline the claim

outcome.text: You insist that care deserves thanks as well as prayer. Church standing improves; you do not manufacture a new miracle to explain your humility.

title: A MOTHER TAKES ILL
text: {{mother}} is seriously ill. The herb-wife offers a costly treatment without a promise. Your mother objects to the expense before allowing herself to ask whether it might work.

choices.label: Fund the uncertain treatment (15g; she may die)

success.text: The treatment succeeds. {{mother}} recovers enough to complain about the fee, a sound you had been afraid of never hearing again.

failure.text: The treatment cannot save {{mother}}. You stay beside the bed and hold a hand no amount of spending can keep warm.

choices.label: Offer care and prayer without the treatment (she may die)

success.text: The fever breaks. {{mother}} credits your company before discussing anybody’s theology.

failure.text: {{mother}} dies despite the care you can give. You do not mistake being unable to pay for having been unwilling to love.

title: A CHILD IS BORN
text: A child has arrived in your household. The smallest person in the room has reorganised every task without speaking a comprehensible word.

outcome.text: A healthy babe joins your household and your line continues. You weep, then panic about feeding it.
You keep the first days close to the household, making promises before making announcements.

title: AN OLD FOE, HUMBLED
text: Sir Roderick appears at your door, greyer and smaller and short of a manor. "I... was wrong about you," he mutters. "About the apple. About all of it."

outcome.text: You clasp his hand. Decades of grudge dissolve in a moment. He weeps; so, secretly, do you.

choices.label: Hand him a single apple, and shut the door

outcome.text: You give him one apple. "Now we are even," you say. The door closes. Petty? Perhaps. Satisfying? Immensely.

title: A SQUALLING ARRIVAL
text: Your mother sits you down with a strange smile. By harvest, you will not be the only small person in this cottage.

outcome.text: A sibling is born! Loud, wrinkled, and immediately beloved. You vow to teach them everything about turnips.
A sibling is born anyway. You sulk magnificently, but the baby grips your finger and your cold heart thaws a little.

title: THE SMITH’S CHILD
text: Another child keeps finding reasons to pass your fence. Today the reason is a pebble that has been kicked in the same small circle for most of the morning.

outcome.text: You split your turnip and gained a friend for life. The finest trade you will ever make.

choices.label: Challenge them to a pebble contest

success.text: You lost the contest on purpose (mostly) and won a friend. Cunning diplomacy.

failure.text: You won too hard and gloated too long. They stomped off. The pebble remains your only trophy.

outcome.text: Sir Quackbeard hissed. The smith’s child fled. Your social circle remains: one goose.

title: A KINDRED SPIRIT
text: A traveller laughs at your worst joke and stays for the explanation. By the time you share a bench, you know the kindness was deliberate.

outcome.text: Ale flowed, tales grew taller, and by closing time you had sworn eternal friendship twice. Once even sober.

choices.label: Swap stories but guard your purse

outcome.text: A fine evening of talk. You part warmly, but strangers stay strangers when the purse stays shut.

title: A DEBT OF STEEL
text: In the training yard a falling practice beam nearly brains another squire, and you shove them clear at the last instant.

choices.label: Help them up and make light of it

outcome.text: "I owe you my skull," they grin, clasping your arm. You have gained a shield-brother, the kind who stands beside you when it costs him something.
They pay you a grudging coin and remember the price of your help more than the help itself.

title: ENVY IN THE LANE
text: A neighbour has begun comparing your fortunes in public. The list contains every piece of your luck and none of the work that preceded it.

success.text: You disarmed his envy with honest flattery about barrels. Not a friend, perhaps, but no longer an enemy.

failure.text: He took your kindness for gloating. The feud is now official; he has already composed insulting verses.

outcome.text: You ignore him. The grudge ferments nicely in its barrel. Aldwin is now, formally, your rival.
Your jibe about his wobbliest barrel drew roars of laughter. Aldwin will never, ever forgive it.

title: THE GREYING COURTIER
text: An experienced courtier offers to teach you which doors to knock on and which invitations mean you are being sent out of the room. The second lesson was expensive to learn.

outcome.text: You gain a mentor who knows where every body at court is buried, and can point to three of them from the window.
At court, kindness is usually bait. You bow out gracefully, and wonder for years what they knew.

title: A LORD TAKES NOTICE
text: A lord offers a place in the retinue, with protection and obligations to be spoken before witnesses. The promise is useful precisely because it will be remembered.

outcome.text: You swear fealty before the hall. A liege’s favour opens doors, and his wars are now your wars.
You decline with careful courtesy. Bramwell nods slowly. Freedom kept, favour lost.

title: THE PESTILENCE COMES
text: A traveller is taken ill in the square. By evening the news has reached every door, growing more certain as the evidence becomes harder to find.

choices.label: Flee to the hills at once

success.text: You fled to the high pastures and waited it out. Lonely and hungry and breathing.

failure.text: You fled, but carried the sickness with you. The fever finds you on the road.

effects.death: Taken by the Pestilence on a lonely hill road.

success.text: You nursed the dying with rags and prayers and somehow did not fall ill. The village calls you blessed.

failure.text: You tended the sick, and the sickness took you in turn. A merciful death, the priest says. He is lying.

effects.death: Died of the Pestilence, tending those who could not be saved.

success.text: You sealed the door and rationed turnips for a grim season. The Pestilence passed you by.

failure.text: It came through the rats, through the very walls. There was no barricade against it.

effects.death: Died of the Pestilence, alone behind a barred door.

title: A WORLD MADE EMPTY
text: The sickness has eased, leaving exhausted households and urgent work. People are counting who is available before agreeing what labour is worth.

choices.label: Ask for wages that reflect the actual shortage

outcome.text: You earn more for urgent work and gain standing among labouring households. No particular neighbour is declared dead merely to explain the wage.

choices.label: Pay to restore a neglected dwelling

outcome.text: You improve your own household’s shelter and standing. You do not acquire somebody else’s cottage simply by noticing its empty door.

choices.label: Help with the ordinary work of recovery

outcome.text: You improve household food and public health conditions through practical aid. The quiet work does not require a triumphant explanation.

title: THE LEVY IS CALLED
text: The levy is called. A spear and a place in the line are offered with considerably more certainty than any account of when you will return.

outcome.text: You march off to war, one frightened spearman among hundreds. The mud is the only certainty.

success.text: You hid among the turnips until the sergeants gave up looking. Coward? Survivor? Both.

failure.text: They found you cowering and dragged you out by the ankle. Now you march AND everyone knows.

outcome.text: A few coins to the sergeant and you keep your skin and your turnips. Money well spent.

title: THE GOOSE IS SUMMONED
text: The reeve summons Sir Quackbeard in a disputed theft. The clerk leaves space for a mark; the goose inspects whether it can be eaten.

outcome.text: You translate three honks as "the baker did it." The baker confesses to avoid further poultry law.
Sir Quackbeard bites the reeve. The court accepts this as strong testimony.
You accuse the pie of tempting honest men. The court pauses, then fines you for nonsense.

title: A PIG ON TRIAL
text: A pig is accused of eating chapel flowers. The court debates intent while the defendant attempts to consume the evidence basket.

success.text: Your speech on floral temptation moves the court. The pig is spared and immediately eats the verdict.

failure.text: Your defense collapses when the accused eats your sleeve.

outcome.text: The pig is sentenced to public shame. It appears immune.

title: HOLY BATHWATER
text: A friar sells holy bathwater that smells of yesterday’s broth. He calls the floating onion a sign that the blessing has taken.

outcome.text: You drink it and feel warmth in the soul, or possibly leek. The friar calls both miracles.

success.text: You find a turnip floating in the relic jar. The crowd turns on him with ladles.

failure.text: The friar declares the turnip a sign. You are booed by people holding soup.

outcome.text: The friar, impressed by your theology of lunch, gives you a heel of bread.

title: THE DOCTOR'S CURE
text: A leech seller offers to treat unpaid rent. His argument is that the landlord cannot demand blood if somebody else has already taken it.

outcome.text: The treatment costs blood and coin without touching the rent. You leave with a clearer sense of what the leeches actually consume.

choices.label: Ask whether the landlord has agreed

outcome.text: The seller has not consulted the landlord. You gain judgement while the leeches continue to make a much simpler living.

choices.label: Sell a false specimen to the seller

outcome.text: You earn six gold and create a fraud charge. A worm in a cup has proved more difficult to defend than to sell.

title: SAINT SOMEBODY'S TOE
text: A seller displays a waxy toe attributed to a saint whose name becomes less certain when you ask for the history of the other nine.

outcome.text: The toe is wax. Your faith wobbles, but your candle supply improves.
Nothing happens. The seller says the toe is shy before crowds.
The priest confiscates the toe, then quietly asks if there were any fingers.

title: THE ALEHOUSE OATH
text: The tavern agrees to dig defensive works before dawn. Nobody has agreed which side of the ditch Swineford ought to occupy.

outcome.text: By dawn you have made a ditch, lost a shoe, and invented a new smell.
You sell shovels at heroic prices. The moat is poor; your purse is excellent.
You wake to find the moat is actually around you.

title: THE MILLER'S TOLL
text: The miller calls his enlarged scoop an improvement in accuracy. It is certainly more accurate at transferring flour into his own store.

success.text: You find a stone hidden in his scoop. The village laughs until flour comes out of their noses.

failure.text: The miller talks faster than his wheel. You leave poorer and dusted white.

outcome.text: You pay quietly. Your revenge ripens like damp grain.

title: THE BELL RINGER'S BET
text: The bell ringer bets that you cannot sleep through matins. He holds the rope like a man whose confidence has a very direct source.

success.text: You sleep like a blessed log. The bell ringer fears you may be part stone.

failure.text: The first bell launches you out of bed and into a bucket.

outcome.text: You ring early. Half the village arrives angry, dressed, and spiritually confused.

title: THE TURNIP ORACLE
text: A root split by frost is being read as a weather omen. The keeper promises an answer before supper, when the evidence will be eaten.

choices.label: Study the crack rather than buy the prophecy

outcome.text: You learn how frost split the root and improve household food planning. The forecast is useful precisely because nobody claims it speaks.

choices.label: Buy it as food and end the performance

outcome.text: You make a meal of the disputed evidence. The household gains food; no prediction is proved merely because you are fed.

title: THE WRONG SPOON
text: The steward gives you a spoon whose use depends on the guest seated above you. You have been placed directly beneath a person who will not eat.

choices.label: Use the spoon and accept the risk of a joke

success.text: You choose correctly and gain a little courtly standing. The spoon performs the undistinguished task it was made for.

failure.text: You choose badly and lose standing. The steward now has a story in which the most important object is cutlery.

choices.label: Use bread and leave the rule untested

outcome.text: You eat neatly with bread and gain a little judgement. The idle guest remains the only person waiting on the spoon.

title: THE JESTER'S BITE
text: The jester has prepared a joke about your boots. The room is waiting to discover whether your power is large enough to survive a small laugh.

outcome.text: You laugh first and steal the sting. The court likes a target who can bow.

success.text: Your reply lands so neatly the jester bows to you. Terrible for him, excellent for your legend.

failure.text: Your comeback limps out and dies near the salt cellar.

title: A VERY OLD FAMILY TREE
text: A clerk offers a royal pedigree with space left for your preferred ancestor. The oldest branch of the family tree is still drying.

outcome.text: You gain three dukes, a saint, and one suspiciously handsome oak tree.
You point out the wet seal. The clerk says your eyesight is lowborn.
Sir Quackbeard is inserted as a Norman baron. Somehow the chart improves.

title: THE GOLDEN FLATTERER
text: A courtier praises your judgement so extensively that the favour he wants has begun to sound overdue.

outcome.text: The praise doubles at once. Your nose is now compared to a noble ship.
He wanted a post, a purse, and your cousin's hand. You give him none and keep your spoon.

title: THE BISHOP'S FISH
text: The bishop claims the largest fish on grounds of spiritual precedence. The dish has become an excellent test of how hungry theology can be.

outcome.text: The bishop takes the fish and a second helping of the argument that got it for him. He blesses you between mouthfuls and has forgotten your name by the fruit.

success.text: You prove the smallest fish is humblest and therefore holiest. The bishop loses appetite and argument, in that order.

failure.text: You confuse a psalm with a recipe. The bishop keeps the fish and the moral high ground.

title: THE SINGING LAWYER
text: A lawyer presents a boundary claim in rhyme. The verse is impeccable, which is awkward because the measurements are not.

success.text: Your couplet wins the room and, somehow, the argument. The clerk copies it into the roll, where it will embarrass someone for a century.

failure.text: You rhyme "acre" with "baker." The judge ages visibly and rules against everyone present.

outcome.text: Everyone thanks you except the lawyer, who was halfway to rhyming "ditch." The case is decided in an hour instead of a season.

title: THE COURT PORTRAIT
text: A painter has rendered your face with dismaying honesty. The clothes are splendid, so no one can claim the same mistake affected the whole canvas.

outcome.text: The court admires your humility. The painter admits he painted the cabbage from memory. It hangs in the great hall for the rest of your life.

memory.note: A famously unflattering portrait hangs where everyone can see it.

outcome.text: The new version has heroic cheekbones and no known relation to you. The first one is not destroyed, merely moved somewhere with worse light.

title: HONOUR OF THE TURNIP
text: A knight mocks the root on your crest. The insult might be harmless if he were not waiting so eagerly to see what you will pay for a reply.

success.text: You strike his shield so hard the turnip becomes fashionable.

failure.text: He knocks you into a cart of actual turnips. The symbolism is unbearable.

outcome.text: You declare the turnip humble, nourishing, and hard to kill. The crowd cheers despite itself.

title: THE SQUIRE'S HELMET
text: A squire has polished your helmet through a thin patch. You can now admire the work from both sides of the metal.

outcome.text: The squire beams and drops the helmet on your foot.
You lecture on care, duty, and not blinding allies with shine.

title: THE PUDDING PRIZE
text: The tourney offers a spur for skill and a pudding for endurance. Competitors are becoming suspicious about which contest is expected to produce more casualties.

success.text: You win the spur and only a modest limp. Chivalry smiles.

failure.text: You lose the bout and land face-first in the prize pudding. The heralds will describe this for years, always at feasts.

memory.note: Unhorsed into a pudding before the whole tourney field.

outcome.text: You win the pudding by terrifying everyone with sincerity, then eat a third of it standing up.

title: THE HORSE SERMON
text: The chaplain blesses the warhorses. One bows its head at exactly the right moment, creating an unfortunate comparison with the riders.

outcome.text: The horse sneezes on you at the amen. The chaplain calls it a sign, and the stable hands start calling you Blessed of the Bay Mare.
It steps on your boot. The debate is settled, and the chaplain writes down that you doubted publicly.

title: A RANSOM IN POULTRY
text: A captured knight’s proposed ransom contains poultry, buttons and an account of why ready coin would be beneath the dignity of his house.

outcome.text: The ducks arrive furious. The promise not to sing proves priceless, and the knight leaves owing you a courtesy he will one day be asked to repay.

memory.note: A knight ransomed himself in poultry and still owes a favour.

success.text: His family pays in coin and apologizes for the ducks. They do not forget being made to apologize.

failure.text: His family sends more ducks. You have negotiated poorly and now keep five ducks.

title: THE RUSTY SWORD RELIC
text: A monk identifies your rusty practice sword as a martyr’s relic. You remember the smith making it, but the monk says certainty can be a spiritual obstacle.

outcome.text: Pilgrims kiss the rust. You feel pious and slightly worried about tetanus.
You keep it. The monk asks if your boot has any sacred blisters.

title: THE DUCKING STOOL HONOUR
text: A village asks you to settle a dispute by ducking both parties. The stated advantage is that nobody needs to listen to them finish.

outcome.text: Justice splashes. Everyone leaves wet, offended, and weirdly satisfied. The village adds your name to the custom.
You listen for an hour and discover the true villain is a missing cheese. Word spreads that you will actually hear a case, which is going to cost you every future afternoon.

title: THE BAD HERALD
text: Your herald announces a title from the rehearsal notes rather than the approved roll. The mistake describes your damp estate with painful accuracy.

choices.label: Accept the damp title and laugh first

outcome.text: You make the mistake safe to laugh at and gain household loyalty. The herald retains a job that suddenly feels much less secure.

memory.note: A herald’s joke became a title you chose to keep.

choices.label: Correct the roll without inventing a punishment

outcome.text: You have the proper title read and lose a little charm. The household learns you value precision even when everyone has heard the alternative.

title: THE FEAST DISASTER
text: At your feast, sauce catches fire just as a guest praises the kitchen’s originality. The cook waits to hear whether this is a compliment or a charge.

outcome.text: You declare it a new French fashion. No one knows enough French to disagree.
The cook bows and points out you ordered "something memorable." Treason by accuracy.

title: YOUR FACE IN GLASS
text: A proposed chapel window gives you a halo and very prominent ears. The glazier says the ears will be less noticeable once people start praying.

outcome.text: You praise the holy light. At sunset, your ears glow across the nave.
The glazier reduces them. The saint beside you now looks disappointed.

title: THE OVERPROUD COUSIN
text: A relative insists the family has always been noble while hiding the household’s old tools. The tools have a more convincing account of the past.

outcome.text: He invents an ancestor who conquered a ditch. The room chooses to believe it, which means someone will eventually check.
You speak warmly of Swineford mud. Half the court laughs; the other half checks its boots. Your cousin does not speak to you until Candlemas.

title: THE REEVE'S PETITION
text: The reeve asks to tax smoke because it passes through your air. His calculation makes a cold, poor household look like a wilful tax evader.

outcome.text: The villagers cheer. The reeve sadly scratches "cloud rent" from his next proposal. The whole village now knows what sort of lord it has, which is worth more than the four shillings.
The treasury gains coin. Every chimney now smokes accusingly, and the reeve begins drafting cloud rent in earnest.

memory.note: You put a tax on chimney smoke and the village has not forgotten.

title: THE FRIAR AND THE PUDDING
text: A friar condemns appetite while concealing a pudding under his robe. A dark patch is developing exactly where the argument is weakest.

outcome.text: The pudding drops at the word "temptation." The sermon ends early and sticky, and the friar remembers precisely who was pointing.
You cough loudly while he rescues dessert. He blesses you with grateful crumbs and, more usefully, owes you a silence of your own one day.

memory.note: A friar owes you a kindness for a pudding nobody mentioned.

title: THE UPSIDE-DOWN FLAG
text: A sickness flag hangs the wrong way up. Two factions are arguing over the meaning of a knot nobody has offered to untie.

outcome.text: You fix the flag. The argument moves to whether you used the blessed ladder, and will still be running at Lammas.
You declare the flag cannot read itself. This is called wisdom by three people and heresy by one, and it is the one who writes letters.

title: THE PARDONER'S BUNDLE
text: A pardoner offers forgiveness among the combs and trinkets on his stall. He recommends buying it before the afternoon prices rise.

outcome.text: He forgives you for sins you had not planned yet. Efficient, if troubling. You keep the paper, which is the part that will matter.

memory.note: You hold a pardoner’s letter for sins not yet committed.

outcome.text: He flees at the word "receipt." The crowd learns a valuable theology of paperwork, and repeats the story at every fair for a decade.

title: THE HEIR'S FIRST WORD
text: A young child in your household offers an early word that sounds like “goat.” You are asked to judge whether this demonstrates genius or somebody else’s example.

outcome.text: You declare the child prophetic. The family begins watching goats for omens.
Your spouse blames you back with better evidence.

title: FATHER'S TALL TALE
text: {{father}} tells a story in which the enemy gets larger every time the bowl is refilled. {{mother}} remembers being present and is finding the new numbers difficult.

outcome.text: Your father glows with pride and retells it as eight taxmen.
Your mother describes the goose victory in brutal detail. Your father studies the floor.

title: SLEEPING THROUGH SERMON
text: {{spouse}} nods off during the sermon and snores into a pause designed for moral reflection. The reflection spreads to your bench.

outcome.text: They wake, nod gravely, and pretend the snore was theological agreement.
The priest takes it personally. The pew takes it loudly.

title: THE WRONG DOOR
text: A marker has mistaken your door for one under sickness watch. The apology is being delivered from a distance the mistake itself has made unnecessary.

outcome.text: You scrub until the door is cleaner than your soul.
No one visits for weeks. Peaceful, except for the screaming outside.

title: THE BELL ARGUMENT
text: The bell ringer asks what a sickness warning ought to sound like. Everyone wants a warning that is accurate and not intended for them.

outcome.text: The bells ring bright over a frightened village. For a moment people breathe easier, and afterwards they remember who chose the sound of that year.
The bells terrify everyone except the sickness, which has poor manners. Three households leave Swineford rather than hear them again.

title: THE BACKWARDS BANNER
text: Your unit’s banner has been sewn backwards. The commander says the enemy must not be allowed to learn how literally the company can face the wrong way.

outcome.text: You fix the banner and earn respect from everyone who can read cloth.
The captain loves it. Confusion, he says, is half of war and most of command.

title: COUNTING ARROWS
text: The quartermaster’s arrow count changes every time a bundle is opened. He proposes blessing the total rather than counting the shafts.

outcome.text: You count thirty-seven arrows and one suspicious knitting needle.
The arrows remain thirty-seven. The needle seems holier.

title: THE COWARDLY DRUM
text: The war drum splits before the muster. The drummer gives it an honourable speech and asks whether a barrel might be promoted into the vacancy.

outcome.text: The men laugh, then cheer. Morale is a strange stew.
You beat a barrel into service. It sounds terrible, but so does war.

title: A VACANT BARONY
text: A border barony lacks a lord. The council wants coin, manners, and someone foolish enough to live near raiders.

outcome.text: The seal is yours. Your patent is entered in the royal register; your household now holds a barony.
You smile, bow, and keep your purse closed. The chance may come again, if death does not get bored first.

title: OATH DAY
text: Your tenants gather to swear loyalty. They look hungry, hopeful, and very aware of your boots.

outcome.text: You promise justice first and coin second. The crowd cheers like people who have heard promises before, but want to believe.
You remind them that loyalty has fees. The strong nod. The poor stare at the mud.

title: A FACE FROM SWINEFORD
text: An old neighbor asks for mercy after stealing grain from your storehouse.

outcome.text: You send them home with grain enough for winter. Nobles call it weakness. Everyone else calls it dinner.
The stocks fill by sunset. Your barns remain full, and your halls grow quieter.

title: RAIDERS AT THE BORDER
text: Smoke rises from the edge of your lands. Your steward asks whether to muster riders or count losses.

success.text: You drive the raiders off and return with a dented helm and a louder legend.

failure.text: The raid breaks your line. You survive, but the songs do not flatter your horse.

outcome.text: Paid guards do paid work. The raiders find easier prey, and your villagers sleep.

title: TAX SEASON
text: The ledgers are thin. Your steward suggests squeezing the villages. He says squeezing with a smile helps.

outcome.text: The treasury groans, but the people bless your name in every bakehouse.
Coin pours in. So do complaints. You discover complaints cannot be minted.

title: A POWERFUL MATCH
text: A neighboring house offers marriage ties. The portrait is flattering. Suspiciously flattering.

outcome.text: The wedding is grand, costly, and full of relatives counting your plates.
You decline with such grace that only half the family vows revenge.

title: LESSONS FOR AN HEIR
text: A child in your household asks how to rule. A dangerous question from someone holding a wooden sword.

outcome.text: You teach that power is lent, not owned. The child nods, then pardons a biscuit thief.
You teach that crowns are held by steady hands. The child immediately orders the spoon drawer inspected.

title: THE COURT POET
text: A poet offers to make you immortal in verse. The first draft rhymes "baron" with "barren."

outcome.text: The second draft flatters your jaw, your wisdom, and a battle you barely attended.
The poet leaves, loudly comparing you to damp porridge. Annoying, but accurate in meter.

title: ROYAL FAVOR
text: A royal messenger praises your household. Praise from above is rarely free.

outcome.text: The crown remembers your generosity, which is the polite word for payment.
Your letter is loyal, cheap, and only slightly damp from panic.

title: SICKNESS IN THE VILLAGES
text: A fever moves through your lands. The physician asks whether the poor are worth expensive herbs.

outcome.text: Herbs, bread, and clean straw save more lives than any sermon. People remember.
Your household survives behind locked gates. Outside, the bells do not stop.

title: A CLAIM TO THE CROWN
text: Your documented claim reaches the council while the reigning monarch’s mandate falters. The genealogist recommends bringing witnesses rather than fresh ink.

success.text: Banners rise. Rivals kneel. Somehow, impossibly, the crown rests on your head.

failure.text: The claim collapses under laughter and steel. You flee with fewer friends and lighter coffers.

outcome.text: You tuck the family tree away. Some branches are best left unclimbed.

title: FIRST DAY WITH THE CROWN
text: Everyone bows. Everyone wants something. The crown is heavier than it looked on other heads.

outcome.text: You promise peace, bread, and fewer public hangings. The hall applauds cautiously.
You promise order. The hall applauds very quickly, which is almost the same as love.

title: THE EMPTY TREASURY
text: s=>`The royal treasury contains ${s.world.court?.treasury??0} gold, two moths, and a note blaming the previous ruler.`

outcome.text: Wealthy households contribute coin and grain to the royal appeal. The kingdom eats, and the donors keep very careful receipts.
The treasury fattens overnight. So does the list of people muttering near tavern doors.

title: REBELLION
text: A duke declares you unfit to rule. Rude, dangerous, and annoyingly well funded.

success.text: The rebellion breaks. You return with torn banners and a kingdom that suddenly remembers its manners.

failure.text: Your army scatters. The council recognises a rival, removes your seal and sends you into exile.

outcome.text: You offer mercy with one hand and hold guards behind the door with the other. It works.

title: ROYAL PROGRESS
text: You ride through the kingdom so people may cheer, complain, or throw root vegetables from a patriotic distance.

outcome.text: Your ears ache, but your people feel seen. Even the beet-thrower bows.
The route is shorter, cleaner, and less informative. Royal wrists are delicate things.

title: THE HEIR QUESTION
text: Courtiers whisper about succession. They do this loudly enough to be helpful and insulting.

outcome.text: The court exhales. A named heir is a shield against chaos, and a target for everyone ambitious.
Mystery has power. It also has daggers.

title: A GRAND FEAST
text: Foreign envoys arrive. The cook asks whether to serve modest dignity or edible showing off.

outcome.text: The tables groan, the envoys beam, and someone writes a ballad about the pudding.
The meal is plain, honest, and described by envoys as "educational."

title: JUSTICE DAY
text: Two nobles argue over land. Both have witnesses. Both witnesses look purchased.

outcome.text: You untangle lies until truth limps into view. The court hates how long fairness takes.
The richer house wins, naturally. Justice wears a very expensive hat today.

title: SWINEFORD REMEMBERS
text: Your birth village sends a gift: a turnip wearing a tiny crown.

outcome.text: You laugh until the court dares to join in. Swineford receives a new well and unbearable pride.
The turnip is removed. Unfortunately, jokes grow better underground.

title: THE HOLY CROWN
text: A bishop suggests your rule needs divine polish. He has incense, hymns, and a very large invoice.

outcome.text: The rite dazzles the realm. Even skeptics bow while checking where the smoke comes from.
You decline. The bishop looks wounded, which is a skill bishops practice.

title: A KNIFE IN THE CURTAIN
text: At midnight, a curtain sneezes. Curtains should not know how.

success.text: Your guards seize the assassin. Loyalty, it turns out, is cheaper than a funeral.

failure.text: The guards are late. The knife is not.

effects.death: Assassinated behind a curtain. A poor review for the guards.

outcome.text: You survive the night and wake shaped like a soup pot.

title: YEARS UPON THE THRONE
text: You have ruled long enough that young courtiers think you were born wearing the crown.

outcome.text: Bells ring from coast to border. For one bright day, even your enemies pretend to enjoy you.
You accept the praise with a small nod. The crown has taught you the value of neck muscles.

title: THE WEARY CROWN
text: Your bones ache. Your heir is ready enough. The throne looks more like a chair every year.

outcome.text: You lay the crown down and live to hear people miss you. A rare royal victory.
You grip the throne until your knuckles pale. The court smiles the way knives smile.

title: A LAW FOR COMMONERS
text: A clerk proposes a law protecting common folk from noble whims. Nobles call this the end of civilization.

outcome.text: The common folk cheer. The nobles sulk. This is how you know the ink mattered.
The law vanishes into a drawer deep enough to have weather.

title: WHAT WILL THEY SAY?
text: A chronicler asks how history should remember you. A dangerous thing, history.

outcome.text: The chronicler writes of mercy, bread, and a crown that remembered the mud.
The chronicler writes carefully. Very carefully. Your enemies are described in the past tense.
The chronicler sighs with relief and begins with the turnip fields.

title: THE BISHOP ADMIRES THY FALCON
text: The bishop stops mid-procession to admire your hunting falcon, and asks its breeding in a tone that is not entirely about birds.

outcome.text: He is delighted and slightly embarrassed, and a bishop in that condition is worth a great deal. Your name reaches the diocese before you do.
She takes a heron in front of the whole procession. The bishop talks about it for years and never once offers to buy her.
He pays it without blinking, which tells you the price was too low. You have coin and he has a story about a grasping fellow from Swineford.

title: A HORSE WORTH TAKING
